title: The only curse word I grew up knowing wasn’t a swear word.
contentSeed:
You can’t.

Growing up differently-abled, I heard those two words more than I heard my own name.

You can’t do that.

You can’t go there.

You can’t live independently.

You can’t travel.

You can’t have a career.

You can’t make a difference.

Sometimes those words came from strangers who didn’t know me.

Sometimes they came from people who genuinely loved me and wanted to protect me.

Sometimes they came from doctors, teachers, or people who believed they were simply being realistic.

None of them meant to hurt me.

But they all had something in common.

They had already decided what my life would look like before I ever had the chance to.

For a long time, I wondered if they were right.

When enough people tell you “you can’t,” it becomes easy to wonder if maybe they’re seeing something you don’t.

But over time, I realized something.

Most people weren’t describing my abilities.

They were describing the limits of their own imagination.

Every “you can’t” became a crossroads.

I could either accept someone else’s definition of my future, or I could discover it for myself.

So I chose to try.

Not because I wanted to prove people wrong.

But because I refused to let someone else’s expectations become my reality.

I didn’t know exactly what my future would look like.

I only knew I wasn’t willing to let someone else write it for me.

Today, I’m the Founder & CEO of Light Upon Light, a nonprofit dedicated to helping differently-abled people through advocacy, accessibility, and equality, while changing society’s perception of these honorable individuals through education.

Every school we visit, every partnership we build, every conversation we have, and every life we touch exists because I chose not to accept “you can’t” as the final answer.

Ironically, many of the things people once told me I couldn’t do are now the very things I spend my life doing.

That doesn’t mean I can do everything.

There are things I genuinely cannot do, and that’s okay.

Being differently-abled doesn’t mean pretending limitations don’t exist.

It means refusing to let those limitations define your worth, your purpose, or your potential.

There’s a difference.

The greatest barriers I’ve faced haven’t always been physical.

Many of them have been assumptions.

Assumptions that I couldn’t lead.

That I couldn’t contribute.

That I couldn’t build.

That I couldn’t belong.

Those assumptions are often far more disabling than my condition itself.

That’s why those two words have always felt like a curse to me.

Not because the words themselves are offensive.

But because they have the power to steal possibility before someone has even had the chance to try.

Imagine hearing “you can’t” throughout your childhood.

Imagine carrying those words into adulthood.

Imagine how many dreams are abandoned, not because they were impossible, but because someone convinced another human being they weren’t capable enough to pursue them.

Words matter.

Especially the ones we speak over children.

Especially the ones we speak over differently-abled people.

Instead of saying, “You can’t,” what if we asked,

“How can we make this possible?”

That single shift changes everything.

Sometimes the greatest act of inclusion isn’t removing every barrier overnight.

It’s refusing to become one.

So if there’s one thing I hope you take away from my story, it’s this:

Never let someone else’s “you can’t” become your own.

Because the future isn’t built by people who never heard those words.

It’s built by the people who heard them…

and chose to keep going anyway.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light

title: It’s Not Hate. It’s Something Harder to Admit.
excerpt: Most people aren’t uncomfortable around differently-abled people because they’re cruel.
contentSeed:
Most people aren’t uncomfortable around differently-abled people because they’re cruel.

They’re uncomfortable because they don’t know what to do.

They don’t know whether to offer help, ask questions, or pretend nothing is different. So instead, they create distance.

That distance may seem harmless.

But to the person on the receiving end, it can feel incredibly lonely.

I’ve spent my life watching people change the moment they notice my wheelchair.

Some avoid eye contact.

Some speak to the person beside me instead of speaking to me.

Others become overly cautious, afraid they’ll say the wrong thing.

For a long time, I wondered if there was something wrong with me.

There wasn’t.

The problem wasn’t me.

It was unfamiliarity.

No one is born uncomfortable around differently-abled people.

Children prove that every day.

They ask honest questions. They’re curious, not judgmental. They don’t see someone who needs pity — they simply see someone who is different.

Then society teaches them that disability is something not to talk about.

Don’t stare.

Don’t ask questions.

Don’t bring it up.

So people grow up without ever learning how to interact naturally with differently-abled people. When they finally do, uncertainty replaces confidence.

I don’t believe most people have bad intentions.

I believe they’re afraid of making a mistake.

They’re worried they’ll offend someone.

They’re unsure whether they should help.

Ironically, that fear often creates the very thing they’re trying to avoid: exclusion.

Sometimes saying hello is better than saying nothing at all.

There is another reason we rarely talk about.

Meeting a differently-abled person reminds us that life is fragile.

An accident.

An illness.

A diagnosis.

In a single moment, anyone’s life can change.

That’s an uncomfortable truth.

Sometimes people aren’t reacting to the person in front of them.

They’re reacting to what that person reminds them about themselves.

Here’s the truth.

Differently-abled people don’t expect perfection.

We don’t expect everyone to know the right words.

We simply want to be treated like human beings.

If you’re unsure whether someone needs help, ask.

If they say no, respect that.

If you’re curious, ask respectfully.

Most of us would rather answer an honest question than be avoided because someone was too afraid to start a conversation.

The greatest barriers aren’t always stairs or heavy doors.

Sometimes they’re assumptions.

Sometimes they’re silence.

Sometimes they’re the invisible wall that forms when people don’t know how to interact with someone who is different.

The good news is that invisible walls can be broken.

It starts with something remarkably simple.

A smile.

A conversation.

A willingness to see the person before the wheelchair, the diagnosis, or the label.

Because behind every differently-abled person is exactly what has always been there:

A human being.

Not waiting to be pitied.

Not waiting to inspire you.

Simply waiting to be seen.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light

title: Should I Offer Help to Someone in a Wheelchair? The Answer Is Simpler Than You Think.
excerpt: I can’t count how many times someone has looked at me, wanted to help, and then stopped.
contentSeed:
I can’t count how many times someone has looked at me, wanted to help, and then stopped.

I could see the kindness in their eyes.

I could also see the hesitation.

Should I offer help?

What if I offend her?

So instead of saying anything…

They walked away.

One of the questions I hear most often is:

Is it okay to offer help to someone in a wheelchair?

The answer is much simpler than people think.

Yes.

And for many of us, your kindness is appreciated.

The only thing we ask is this:

Ask before you help.

Kindness Is Welcome. Assumptions Are Not.

Most people aren’t afraid of helping.

They’re afraid of helping the wrong way.

They don’t want to seem disrespectful.

They don’t want to say the wrong thing.

Ironically, that fear often creates distance where kindness could have created connection.

The truth is, you don’t need perfect words.

You don’t need special training.

You don’t need to understand everything about disability.

You simply need to ask.

One Simple Question Changes Everything

The easiest way to offer help is also the most respectful.

Simply ask:

Would you like a hand?

That’s it.

No complicated script.

No awkward explanation.

No guessing.

Just a genuine question.

If the answer is yes, wonderful.

If the answer is no, smile and continue the conversation.

Respecting someone’s answer is just as important as offering your help.

A Wheelchair Is Personal

One mistake people often make is grabbing someone’s wheelchair or beginning to push without asking.

Although it’s usually done with good intentions, it can feel unsettling.

A wheelchair isn’t just a piece of equipment.

It’s part of how someone moves through the world.

Imagine someone suddenly grabbing your arm and deciding where you should go.

Most people would feel surprised.

The same respect applies here.

Always ask first.

Don’t Be Afraid of Getting It Wrong

One of the greatest barriers to inclusion isn’t hate.

It’s fear.

Fear of offending someone.

Fear of saying the wrong thing.

Fear of making an awkward moment even more awkward.

But kindness spoken imperfectly will almost always be received better than silence driven by fear.

Most differently-abled people don’t expect perfection.

We simply appreciate being treated with the same respect, dignity, and humanity as everyone else.

What Most Differently-Abled People Want

People often ask me,

“What’s the right thing to do?”

The answer isn’t a perfect script.

It’s respect.

Say hello.

Make eye contact.

Speak directly to us, not only to the person we’re with.

Offer help if it seems appropriate.

Accept our answer.

Then continue the conversation naturally.

Because before we’re differently-abled…

We’re people.

People with careers.

Families.

Dreams.

Humor.

Goals.

And stories worth knowing.

Inclusion Begins With Ordinary Moments

Many people think inclusion starts with major policy changes, accessibility laws, or expensive renovations.

Those things absolutely matter.

But inclusion also begins in the ordinary moments.

A smile.

A conversation.

A question.

A willingness to treat another human being with dignity.

Sometimes creating a more inclusive world is as simple as asking,

Would you like a hand?

That question says something powerful.

“I see you.”

“I respect your independence.”

“And if you’d like help, I’m here.”

Kindness is rarely offensive.

Assumptions are.

The next time you see someone who might need assistance, don’t let uncertainty stop you from showing compassion.

Simply ask.

You may make someone’s day a little easier.

And together, those small moments create the kind of world we all deserve.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light

title: One Conversation Can Change a Lifetime.
excerpt: Most people think life changes because of the big moments.
contentSeed:
Most people think life changes because of the big moments.

Graduating.

Getting married.

Starting a new job.

Moving somewhere new.

Those moments certainly matter.

But over the years, I’ve learned something different.

Sometimes…

Life changes because someone decided to start a conversation.

A conversation can introduce you to a new opportunity.

A new friendship.

A new perspective.

A new purpose.

Or simply remind you that you’re not alone.

We rarely realize it in the moment.

But one conversation can quietly change the direction of an entire life.

The Conversations We Never Forget

If you think back over your own life, there’s probably a conversation you’ll never forget.

Maybe someone believed in you when you didn’t believe in yourself.

Maybe someone gave you encouragement at exactly the right time.

Maybe someone challenged the way you saw the world.

The conversation may have lasted only a few minutes.

But its impact lasted for years.

Words have a remarkable way of staying with us long after the conversation ends.

Every Person Is Carrying a Story

One of the greatest lessons I’ve learned is that every person you meet is carrying a story you cannot see.

A struggle.

A dream.

A fear.

A hope.

That’s why conversations matter.

You never know what someone is facing behind a smile.

You never know when a simple question like,

“How are you?”

might be exactly what someone needed to hear.

Listening can be just as powerful as speaking.

Sometimes people don’t need advice.

They simply need someone willing to care.

Curiosity Changes Everything

Many people avoid conversations because they’re afraid they’ll say the wrong thing.

They overthink.

They hesitate.

Then they walk away.

But meaningful conversations don’t begin with perfect words.

They begin with genuine curiosity.

A question.

A smile.

A willingness to listen.

That’s all it takes.

Every friendship begins with a conversation.

Every partnership begins with a conversation.

Every movement begins with a conversation.

You Never Know Who Needs You Today

You may never know the impact of the conversations you have.

The person you encourage today might remember your words for the rest of their life.

The person you welcome today might finally feel like they belong.

The person you listen to today might leave with hope they didn’t have before.

That’s the beautiful thing about human connection.

We don’t always see the difference we’re making.

But that doesn’t mean it isn’t happening.

One Conversation Can Change a Lifetime

The next time you have the opportunity to speak with someone…

Don’t underestimate the moment.

Introduce yourself.

Ask the question.

Listen with intention.

Show kindness.

Because while it may feel like an ordinary conversation to you…

It could become an extraordinary moment for someone else.

One conversation can open a door.

One conversation can restore hope.

One conversation can build understanding.

And sometimes…

One conversation can change a lifetime.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light

title: I Was Denied a Cup of Tea Because of My Disability.
excerpt: It wasn’t expensive. It wasn’t rare. It wasn’t about the tea.
contentSeed:
It wasn’t expensive.

It wasn’t rare.

It wasn’t about the tea.

It was what the tea represented.

I remember sitting there, watching everyone else receive a cup.

Then came my turn. There wasn’t one for me. Not because they ran out. Not because they forgot.

But because someone looked at my wheelchair and quietly decided I didn’t need one.

It lasted only a moment.

Yet that moment stayed with me for years.

People often think discrimination always arrives with shouting, anger, or obvious cruelty.

Sometimes…

It arrives with silence.

A small decision. A simple assumption.

Something so ordinary that almost everyone else forgets it happened.

Except the person living it.

It Was Never About the Tea

Losing a cup of tea wasn’t what hurt.

What hurt was the message hidden behind it.

It made me wonder if people saw my wheelchair before they saw me.

If they assumed I needed less.

Expected less.

Deserved less.

The tea became something much bigger.

It became a symbol of dignity.

Of belonging.

Of being treated like everyone else.

That Moment Could Have Made Me Bitter

For a while, I carried that moment with me.

I could have allowed it to become another reason to lose hope.

Instead…

It became a reason to build something.

I realized I wasn’t the only differently-abled person carrying invisible moments like this.

Moments that quietly tell people they don’t belong.

Moments that slowly shape how they see themselves.

I couldn’t change what happened that day.

But I could help create a world where fewer people experience it.

A Cup of Tea Started a Movement

In 2024, I founded Light Upon Light.

Not because of a cup of tea.

Because of what that cup represented.

Every person deserves dignity,  respect and deserve to belong.

Our work isn’t really about wheelchairs.

Or accessibility, policies.

Those things matter.

But they’re only part of the story.

Our mission is about changing the way people see one another.

Because true inclusion begins long before a ramp is built.

It begins in the human heart.

Every Human Being Deserves a Cup of Tea

People sometimes ask why a cup of tea became such an important symbol to me.

The answer is simple.

It reminds me that the smallest moments often reveal the biggest truths.

A cup of tea says,

You’re welcome here.

You belong. I see you.

That’s the kind of world we’re trying to build.

One where no one is overlooked because they’re differently-abled.

One where dignity is never optional.

One where every human being is treated with the respect they deserve.

Because in the end…

It was never about the tea.

It was always about the person holding the cup.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light

title: For a Few Hours, I Stopped Wondering Whether I Belonged.
excerpt: I never expected a public transit agency to make me feel that way.
contentSeed:
I never expected a public transit agency to make me feel that way.

If you had asked me where I’d feel the most accepted, I would’ve pointed to an organization whose mission centered on disability.

I would’ve been wrong.

When Community Transit invited me to speak for their Topics at 12 series, I thought I was there to give a presentation.

I spent time preparing my slides.

Thinking about what I wanted to say.

Hoping my story might make a difference.

What I didn’t realize was that they were about to leave a lasting impression on me.

From the moment I arrived, something felt different.

No one made me feel like I had to prove myself.

No one made me feel defined by my wheelchair.

People greeted me warmly.

They listened with genuine interest.

They valued my ideas.

They respected my experiences.

They treated me the same way they treated everyone else in the room.

It wasn’t dramatic, performative.

It was simply human.

And that’s exactly why it meant so much.

For a few hours…

I stopped wondering whether I belonged.

That feeling is rarer than it should be.

As someone who has spent much of my life navigating spaces that weren’t always built with differently-abled people in mind, you become familiar with the quiet moments that remind you you’re different.

Sometimes it’s a look or an assumption or being spoken to differently or being overlooked altogether.

Those moments don’t always make headlines.

But they stay with you.

Which is why genuine belonging is so powerful.

Community Transit didn’t just invite me to speak.

They created an environment where I felt comfortable enough to simply be myself.

That experience reminded me of something I’ll never forget.

Belonging isn’t created by policies alone.

It isn’t created by mission statements.

It isn’t created by the words hanging on a wall.

Belonging is created by people.

By the way we welcome someone.

By the way we listen.

By the way we make others feel.

That’s what I’ll remember most about that day.

Not the presentation.

Not the slides.

Not even standing in front of the room.

I’ll remember how I felt.

Seen. Respected. Valued. Human.

At Light Upon Light, we’re working toward a world where differently-abled people are seen not for their disabilities or diagnoses, but simply as human beings - just like everyone else.

Because everyone deserves to know what genuine belonging feels like.

And I hope one day…

No one has to wonder whether they belong in the first place.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light
